title: Design exercise: RAG service (retrieval-augmented generation)
summary: An AI-era design exercise: an internal question-answering service over a company's documents with citations, strict permissions and per-team evaluation. The reference answer sizes chunks, vectors and daily tokens from stated assumptions, uses hybrid retrieval with contextual chunks and a reranker, filters by permission before the model sees text, and treats the vector index as a rebuildable derived view. Converted by hand from the module outline's reference answer; every number and source is kept.

exercise.prompt: Design an internal question-answering service over a company's documents (wikis, tickets, PDFs). A user asks a question and gets an answer with citations to the documents it came from. Several teams will put their own document sets on it.

constraints.heading: Functional
constraints.body: Ingest documents from several sources with incremental updates; answer a question with citations; respect document permissions (a user only gets answers from documents they may read); teams can evaluate answer quality on their own question sets.

constraints.heading: Scale (assumption)
constraints.body: 2 million documents, average 20 kB of text, growing 2 percent per month; 20,000 questions per day, peak 2 per second; 50 teams. Chosen for the exercise; derive the chunk count, the vector volume and the daily token volume yourself.

constraints.heading: Targets (assumption)
constraints.body: First token of the answer within 2 s at p50 and 5 s at p95; retrieval under 300 ms at p95; new or changed documents searchable within 15 minutes; model spend bounded per team.

constraints.heading: Non-goals
constraints.body: Training or fine-tuning models, agents that take actions, chat memory beyond one conversation.

clarifying_questions.question: Which model provider, and can it change?
clarifying_questions.answer: Hosted provider now, must be swappable; the service calls it through a gateway (see the LLM gateway exercise).

clarifying_questions.question: How strict are permissions?
clarifying_questions.answer: Strict: a retrieved chunk is filtered by the asker's access before it reaches the model; permission data comes from the source systems.

clarifying_questions.question: What counts as good?
clarifying_questions.answer: Teams define question sets with expected sources; retrieval recall and answer faithfulness are measured.

clarifying_questions.question: Can documents be deleted?
clarifying_questions.answer: Yes; deletion must remove chunks and embeddings within the same 15 minutes.

clarifying_questions.question: Budget?
clarifying_questions.answer: Stated per team per month in tokens.

body.heading: Derived numbers: documents, chunks, vectors
body.body: Text: 2 million times 20 kB is 40 GB. Chunks: at about 500 tokens (roughly 2 kB) per chunk, 10 chunks per document, 20 million chunks. Embeddings: at 1,024 dimensions of 4-byte floats, 4 kB per vector, 80 GB of vectors before compression; an HNSW index adds graph memory on top, so a single machine serving the whole index in memory is large; sharding by team (most teams are small) and quantization (the FAISS wiki) bring it down.

body.heading: Derived numbers: the query path and tokens
body.body: Embed the question (one model call of a few hundred tokens), retrieve top 50 by vector plus top 50 by keyword, rerank to 8, build a prompt of about 6,000 tokens, generate about 400 tokens. At 20,000 questions per day that is roughly 120 million input tokens and 8 million output tokens per day across the fleet (assumption), which is the dominant cost and the reason for per-team budgets and prompt caching of the fixed instructions (the Claude prompt caching documentation).

body.heading: Derived numbers: ingestion
body.body: 2 percent per month of 2 million is 40,000 documents per month, about one per minute on average with bursts after bulk imports.

body.heading: Container view
body.body: Two pipelines share a document store. Ingestion turns document versions into contextualised chunks, vectors and keyword entries per collection. Query embeds the question, retrieves by vector and keyword in parallel, filters by permission before reranking, and streams a generation through the LLM gateway, logging everything an evaluation needs.

body.heading: Entities
body.body: Collection {id, team, source connectors, permission model}; Document {id, collection, source_uri, version, acl, updated_at}; Chunk {id, document, position, text, context_prefix, embedding, keyword index}; Question {id, user, collection(s), text, retrieved chunk ids, answer, citations, latency, tokens}; EvalSet {team, questions with expected document ids}.

body.heading: API
body.body: POST /ask {question, collections[]} returns a stream of tokens, then {citations[]}; POST /collections/{id}/sync (connector-driven, idempotent per document version); POST /evals/{set}/run returns {recall@k, faithfulness, cost}.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

body.heading: Ingestion path
body.body: Connectors emit document versions onto a change log (the queues and streams lesson; the outbox and CDC lesson when the source is a database). A worker chunks the text, prepends a short context sentence to each chunk (the contextual retrieval technique: the public write-up reports a 49 percent reduction in retrieval failures for contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 and 67 percent with reranking added), embeds in batches, writes vectors to the collection's index and text to the keyword index, and records the document version. A new version replaces the old chunks atomically per document (write new, switch the version pointer, delete old); a deletion removes chunks and vectors and is verified by a periodic reconciliation between the metadata store and the indexes. Permissions are stored per document from the source system's ACL and refreshed by the connector.

steps: Run the vector query and the keyword query in parallel against the collections the user named.
Drop any chunk whose document the user may not read (filter before reranking, so the model never sees forbidden text).
Build the prompt with fixed instructions first (cacheable), then the chunks with ids, then the question.
Stream the generation; extract citations as the chunk ids the model referenced and map them to document URIs.
Log everything needed for evaluation (retrieved ids, answer, tokens, latency) with the question text retained under the team's policy.

body.heading: Retrieval quality as an engineering loop
body.body: The Azure guide structures a RAG build as chunking, enrichment, embedding, retrieval evaluation and end-to-end evaluation. The service makes that a product feature: each team keeps an evaluation set (questions with the documents that should be cited); a run reports recall at k for retrieval and a faithfulness score for the answer; a change to chunking, embedding model or reranker is tested against every team's set before rollout, the way a schema migration is tested. The L3 insight is that the vector index is a derived view that can be rebuilt; the source of truth is the document store with versions, so re-embedding with a new model is a backfill (the migrations lesson), done per collection with the old and new index served side by side until the evals pass.

body.heading: Tenancy, permissions and cost
body.body: One index per collection (team) keeps blast radius and cost attribution simple and makes deletion of a team's data a drop of an index; a few very large collections get sharded indexes with scatter-gather across shards. Permission filtering happens on chunk metadata before reranking; for sources with fine-grained ACLs the filter is a join against the document ACL table, which is why document ids and ACL versions are carried on every chunk. Cost: per-team token budgets enforced at the gateway, prompt caching for the instruction prefix, a smaller model for the reranker, and a per-team dashboard of cost per answered question. Latency: retrieval under 300 ms is the index plus the keyword query plus the rerank; the generation dominates and streams, so the first token target is met by starting generation as soon as the prompt is built.

body.body: 200 million chunks: quantized indexes, sharded by collection then by hash, index build separated from serving with immutable segments; retrieval becomes its own service (the vector search exercise). Multi-language: per-language embedding models and keyword analysers, selected per document. Conversation memory: a short per-conversation context stored by the ask API, not by the index.

interview_frame.text: Requirements: the six clarifying questions, the non-goals, and the numbers aloud: 20 million chunks, 80 GB of vectors, 120 million input tokens per day (all assumptions), 2 questions per second at peak, 15-minute freshness.
Entities and API: Collection, Document, Chunk, Question, EvalSet; the streaming ask endpoint, the idempotent sync endpoint, the evaluation run.
High-level design with the diagram: the two pipelines, one index per collection, the permission filter before the reranker, the gateway in front of the model, the question log that feeds evaluation.

Two deep dives: retrieval quality as an evaluation loop (contextual chunks, hybrid retrieval, rerank, per-team eval sets as a release gate, re-embedding as a backfill), then permissions and tenancy (filter by ACL version before rerank, per-collection indexes, deletion, per-team budgets and cost per answer).
Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan, and the L3 sentence: the index is a derived view; the design is really about the document store, the ACLs and the evaluation loop.
